steps.title: Counting eggs by the crate
steps.display: 1 crate = 30 eggs  |  1 mole = 6.02 × 10^{23} particles
working: Market seller counts crates, not single eggs.
Chemist counts moles, not single atoms or molecules.
steps.narration: At a Nigerian market, sellers pack eggs into crates instead of counting them one by one. Chemists pack tiny particles into moles the same way.

steps.title: Moles from mass, s.t.p. volume, and particles
steps.narration: One mole holds the Avogadro constant, six point zero two times ten to the twenty three particles. Divide mass by molar mass, standard gas volume by twenty two point four, or particle count by the Avogadro constant.

steps.title: Percentage composition by mass
steps.display: % element = \frac{mass of element in 1 mol}{molar mass of compound} × 100%
working: Calcium trioxonitrate(V) (calcium nitrate), Ca(NO_{3})_{2}:
steps.narration: To find percentage composition, add every atom inside brackets to get the molar mass. Divide the total mass of the target element in one mole by the compound molar mass, then multiply by one hundred.

steps.title: Empirical and molecular formula
steps.display: MF = (EF)_{n}  |  n = \frac{M}{m_{EF}}  |  M = 2 × vapour density
steps.narration: For an empirical formula, divide each element mass or percentage by its relative atomic mass, then divide by the smallest mole value to get whole numbers. For the molecular formula, divide molar mass, or twice vapour density, by the empirical mass.

steps.title: Balancing equations and conservation of mass
steps.display: Adjust coefficients only (never subscripts)  |  (s), (l), (g), (aq)
working: Unbalanced: H_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) → H_{2}O(l)
4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on each side (mass conserved)
steps.narration: A balanced chemical equation obeys the law of conservation of mass because atom counts stay equal on both sides. Change coefficients in front of formulae, never subscripts inside them, and write state symbols where aqueous means dissolved in water.

steps.title: Reacting masses and gas volumes
steps.display: n_{unknown} = n_{known} × \frac{coeff_{unknown}}{coeff_{known}}
steps.narration: Never compare grams directly across a reaction. First convert the known mass or volume into moles, multiply by the balanced equation mole ratio, then convert the unknown moles into grams or standard gas volume.

steps.title: Limiting reagent and excess reactant
steps.display: Compare \frac{n_{available}}{coeff} → smallest value is the limiting reagent
working: Mix 3 mol H_{2} with 2 mol O_{2}:
H_{2} limits product (3 mol H_{2}O formed; 0.5 mol O_{2} left)
steps.narration: When two reactants are mixed, the one that runs out first is the limiting reagent and controls how much product forms. Divide each available mole or gas volume by its coefficient; the smaller ratio limits the reaction.

steps.title: Read the reaction and convert given mass to moles
steps.display: 4.8 g Mg + 0.30 mol HCl: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl_{2}(aq) + H_{2}(g). Find V_{s.t.p.}(H_{2}).
working: M(Mg) = 24 g mol^{−1}
n(HCl) = 0.30 mol (given)
steps.narration: Here is our practice problem with magnesium and hydrochloric acid. First convert four point eight grams of magnesium to moles by dividing by twenty four, giving zero point two zero moles of magnesium alongside zero point three zero moles of acid.

steps.title: Identify the limiting reagent
steps.display: 1 mol Mg requires 2 mol HCl
working: 0.20 mol Mg needs 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol HCl
Available HCl = 0.30 mol < 0.40 mol
HCl is the limiting reagent (Mg is in excess)
steps.narration: From the balanced equation, one mole of magnesium needs two moles of acid, so zero point two zero moles need zero point four zero moles. Because only zero point three zero moles of acid are present, acid is the limiting reagent.

steps.title: Use the limiting reagent to find moles and volume of hydrogen
steps.narration: Always calculate product from the limiting reagent. Two moles of hydrochloric acid yield one mole of hydrogen gas, so zero point three zero moles yield zero point one five moles. Multiplying by twenty two point four gives three point three six cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Restate the JAMB past question
steps.display: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 180. Find its molecular formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
working: Assume 100 g sample → 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H, 53.3 g O
Target: molecular formula (M_{r} = 180)
steps.narration: Let us solve this twenty twelve JAMB question step by step. Because percentage composition does not depend on sample size, imagine one hundred grams of the compound so each percentage turns straight into grams of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

steps.title: Divide masses by relative atomic masses
steps.display: n_{element} = \frac{mass}{A_{r}}
steps.narration: Convert each mass into moles of atoms. Divide forty by twelve for carbon, six point seven by one for hydrogen, and fifty three point three by sixteen for oxygen, giving three point three three, six point seven, and three point three three.

steps.title: Divide by the smallest mole value to get the empirical formula
steps.display: Smallest mole amount = 3.33  →  Empirical formula = CH_{2}O
steps.narration: Now divide all three mole numbers by the smallest one, three point three three. You get a clean one to two to one whole number ratio, so the empirical formula is C H two O.

steps.title: Scale the empirical formula to the relative molecular mass
working: Molecular formula = (CH_{2}O)_{6} = C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}
steps.narration: Do not stop at the empirical formula! C H two O has mass thirty, whereas the molecular mass is one hundred and eighty. Dividing one hundred and eighty by thirty gives six, making the molecular formula C six H twelve O six.

steps.title: Diatomic molecules and bracket subscripts
working: H_{2}, N_{2}, O_{2}, F_{2}, Cl_{2}, Br_{2}, I_{2} are diatomic gases.
Ca(NO_{3})_{2} has 1 Ca, 2 N, and 6 O atoms (M = 164).
steps.narration: Many JAMB candidates mistakenly use sixteen grams per mole for oxygen gas or thirty five point five for chlorine gas, forgetting they are diatomic molecules. Also remember a subscript outside brackets multiplies every atom inside the bracket.

steps.title: Empirical formula versus molecular formula and vapour density
steps.display: Wrong: stopping at EF or using M = VD  |  Right: M = 2 × VD, then MF = (EF)_{n}
steps.narration: A frequent exam trap offers the empirical formula as a distractor when the molecular formula is asked, or vice versa. Always check whether you need the simplest ratio or the true molecule, and always double vapour density to get relative molecular mass.

steps.title: Equation ratios and excess left over
steps.display: Wrong: 1000 cm^{3} H_{2} + 300 cm^{3} O_{2} → 700 cm^{3} left  |  Right: 600 cm^{3} used, 400 cm^{3} left
steps.narration: Do not subtract reactant volumes one to one or stop at the volume that reacted! Use the balanced equation ratio first, then check whether JAMB asks for the product formed, the volume consumed, or the excess reactant remaining.

steps.title: Moles are the bridge for every chemical calculation
steps.display: Given (mass, volume, particles) → Moles → Balanced mole ratio → Target
working: Check subscripts, balance the equation, find the limiting reagent, then solve.
steps.narration: Convert whatever you are given into moles first, follow the balanced equation ratio through the limiting reagent, and then convert cleanly into the mass, volume, or particle count requested.

quickCheck.stem: Which sample contains the same number of constituent molecules as the number of atoms in 24 g of magnesium? Use Mg = 24, H = 1, O = 16 and Cl = 35.5.

options.why: M(H_{2}) = 2 g mol^{−1}, so 1 g of H_{2} is only 0.5 mol of molecules, half of 1 mol.
Oxygen gas is diatomic with M(O_{2}) = 32 g mol^{−1}, so 16 g is only 0.5 mol of molecules.
24 g of Mg is \frac{24}{24} = 1 mol of atoms, and 32 g of O_{2} is \frac{32}{32} = 1 mol of molecules, so both contain N_{A} particles.
Chlorine gas is diatomic with M(Cl_{2}) = 71 g mol^{−1}, so 35.5 g is only 0.5 mol of molecules.

steps.title: Hot sun on a car tyre
steps.display: Heat up trapped air → faster molecules → more wall hits → higher pressure
working: Pump air into a tyre, press harder to shrink it, or warm it in afternoon sun.
steps.narration: Leave an inflated car tyre in hot Nigerian afternoon sun and the trapped air molecules speed up, hammering the rubber harder so the pressure rises.

steps.title: Kelvin conversion and standard conditions (s.t.p.)
working: Absolute zero = 0 K (−273 °C)
1 mol ideal gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^{3} (1 dm^{3} = 1000 cm^{3})
steps.narration: Every gas law temperature must be in kelvin, never Celsius. Add two hundred and seventy three to convert Celsius to kelvin, so standard conditions mean two hundred and seventy three kelvin and one atmosphere, or seven hundred and sixty millimetres of mercury.

steps.title: Boyle's law, Charles's law, and the pressure law
steps.display: Boyle (const T): P_{1}V_{1} = P_{2}V_{2}  |  Charles (const P): \frac{V_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{V_{2}}{T_{2}}  |  Pressure (const V): \frac{P_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{P_{2}}{T_{2}}
working: Boyle: P doubled → V halved (P_{1} = 2 atm, V_{1} = 6 dm^{3} → P_{2} = 3 atm, V_{2} = 4 dm^{3})
Pressure law: P_{1} = 1.0 atm at 300 K → at 600 K, P_{2} = 2.0 atm
steps.narration: For a fixed mass of gas, Boyle's law says pressure and volume vary inversely at constant temperature. Charles's law links volume directly to kelvin temperature at constant pressure, while the pressure law links pressure directly to kelvin temperature at constant volume.

steps.title: General gas equation and ideal gas equation
working: Combined law handles changing P, V, and T for fixed n.
PV = nRT uses R = 0.082 atm dm^{3} K^{−1} mol^{−1} (P in atm, V in dm^{3})
steps.narration: Combine Boyle's and Charles's laws into the general gas equation when pressure, volume, and temperature all change together. When moles are given or wanted, use P V equals n R T and match the gas constant R to your pressure and volume units.

steps.title: Dalton's law of partial pressures
steps.display: P_{total} = P_{1} + P_{2} + ...  |  P_{i} = \frac{n_{i}}{n_{total}} P_{total}  |  P_{dry} = P_{total} − P_{water}
working: Mixture: 1 mol A + 3 mol B at P_{total} = 2.0 atm → P_{A} = \frac{1}{4} × 2.0 = 0.50 atm
Over water at 760 mmHg if P_{water} = 20 mmHg → P_{dry} = 760 − 20 = 740 mmHg
steps.narration: For non-reacting gases in one container, total pressure equals the sum of all partial pressures. Each gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times total pressure, and for a gas collected over water, always subtract saturated water vapour pressure first.

steps.title: Gay-Lussac's law and Avogadro's law
steps.display: Gay-Lussac: reacting gas volumes bear simple whole-number ratios  |  Avogadro: V ∝ n (const T, P)
working: 2CO(g) + O_{2}(g) → 2CO_{2}(g)  (2 vol : 1 vol : 2 vol)
Equal gas volumes at the same T and P hold equal numbers of molecules.
steps.narration: Gay-Lussac's law says reacting gases and gaseous products combine in simple whole-number volume ratios at constant temperature and pressure. Avogadro's law explains why equal volumes of any gases under identical temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.

steps.title: Graham's law of diffusion
working: Compare H_{2} (M = 2) and O_{2} (M = 32):
\frac{r(H_{2})}{r(O_{2})} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{2}} = \sqrt{16} = 4  →  H_{2} diffuses 4 times faster
steps.narration: At constant temperature and pressure, a gas's rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass or vapour density. Lighter molecules move faster, and rate equals volume diffused divided by time taken.

steps.title: List variables and convert Celsius to kelvin
steps.display: A gas occupies 300 cm^{3} at 27 °C and 760 mmHg. Find its volume at 127 °C and 380 mmHg.
steps.narration: Look at what changes in this practice question, pressure, volume, and temperature all change while mass stays fixed. First convert both temperatures to kelvin by adding two hundred and seventy three, giving three hundred kelvin and four hundred kelvin.

steps.title: Rearrange the general gas equation for the final volume
working: Check units: P_{1} and P_{2} are both mmHg; V_{1} is cm^{3}, so V_{2} is cm^{3}.
steps.narration: Because pressure, volume, and temperature all vary, choose the general gas equation. Rearrange cleanly to make the final volume V two the subject, and confirm both pressures use millimetres of mercury so units cancel.

steps.title: Substitute values and check physical sense
steps.narration: Substitute the numbers and notice how neatly three hundred cancels three hundred, while seven hundred and sixty divided by three hundred and eighty equals two. That gives eight hundred cubic centimetres, which makes sense because halving pressure and heating both expand the gas.

steps.title: Restate the JAMB past question
steps.display: A volume of 200 cm^{3} of oxygen diffuses through a porous plug in 50 s. How long will 80 cm^{3} of methane, CH_{4}, take under the same conditions? (O = 16, C = 12, H = 1)
steps.narration: Here is a twenty sixteen JAMB question on Graham's law where the two gases have different volumes. Always compute oxygen's diffusion rate first and work out the molar masses of oxygen gas and methane.

steps.title: Find oxygen's diffusion rate and the Graham's law ratio
steps.narration: Oxygen diffuses two hundred cubic centimetres in fifty seconds, which is four cubic centimetres per second. By Graham's law, methane is lighter so its speed relative to oxygen is the square root of thirty two over sixteen, which is root two.

steps.title: Divide methane's volume by methane's rate to find time
steps.narration: Now divide methane's eighty cubic centimetres by four root two cubic centimetres per second. Eighty over four gives twenty, and twenty divided by root two is ten root two, which is roughly fourteen seconds.

steps.title: Never plug degrees Celsius into a gas law
steps.display: Wrong: T = 20 °C in PV = nRT or Charles's law  |  Right: T = 20 + 273 = 293 K
working: Doubling both P and V quadruples T in Kelvin (273 K → 1092 K).
At 20 °C, n = \frac{8.2 × 2.93}{0.082 × 293} = 1.00 mol (using 20 gives a huge error).
steps.narration: Gas volume and pressure are proportional to kelvin temperature, never Celsius. Using Celsius directly in Charles's law, the combined equation, or P V equals n R T ruins the ratio every time, so add two hundred and seventy three first.

steps.title: Subtract water vapour pressure and check which gas is asked
steps.display: Wrong: P_{dry} = 765 mmHg (wet) or picking P(N_{2}) for P(O_{2})  |  Right: P_{dry} = 765 − 5 = 760 mmHg
working: Gas over water: P_{dry} = P_{total} − P_{water vapour}.
steps.narration: When gas is collected over water, always subtract water vapour pressure before using the gas laws. And in mole-fraction problems, always calculate from the given moles or pressures instead of guessing from memory, and match the right gas.

steps.title: Remember the square root in Graham's law
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{r_{X}}{r_{Y}} = \frac{M_{Y}}{M_{X}} → 2 × 28 = 56  |  Right: \left(\frac{r_{X}}{r_{Y}}\right)^{2} = \frac{M_{Y}}{M_{X}} → 4 × 28 = 112
working: If X (M = 28) diffuses twice as fast as Y, 2 = \sqrt{\frac{M_{Y}}{28}}.
Square both sides: 4 = \frac{M_{Y}}{28} → M_{Y} = 112.
steps.narration: Students often forget the square root in Graham's law and double the molar mass instead of quadrupling it when a gas diffuses twice as fast. Square the rate ratio before solving for molar mass, and compare rates when volumes differ.

steps.title: Kelvin first, dry pressure second, right law third
steps.display: T → Kelvin  |  Gas over water → P_{total} − P_{water}  |  Match P, V, T, n, or \sqrt{M}
working: Convert to kelvin, strip out water vapour if wet, and pick the matching gas law.
steps.narration: Convert every temperature to kelvin first, subtract water vapour pressure when a gas is collected over water, and choose the gas law that matches the changing variables.

quickCheck.stem: A 50 cm^{3} gas sample is collected over water at 10 °C and 765 mmHg. Water vapour pressure is 5 mmHg. What volume would the dry gas occupy at 0 °C and 760 mmHg?

options.why: 49.19 cm^{3} uses too small a kelvin temperature ratio.
48.87 cm^{3} does not match the 273 K to 283 K cooling ratio.
48.55 cm^{3} uses the wet total pressure of 765 mmHg instead of subtracting 5 mmHg.

steps.title: Lime juice meets wood ash water
steps.display: Sour lime (acid) + wood-ash water (alkali) → milder salt + water
working: Sharp sourness vs slippery bitterness
Mix the right amounts → they cancel out
steps.narration: Fresh lime tastes sharply sour while wood ash water feels soapy. Mix the exact right amounts together and they cancel out into milder salt and water.

steps.title: Strong vs weak and basicity
steps.display: Strong: complete ionisation (→)   |   Weak: partial ionisation (⇌)
working: HCl + H_{2}O → H_{3}O^{+} + Cl^{-}  (strong, high conductivity)
CH_{3}COOH + H_{2}O ⇌ H_{3}O^{+} + CH_{3}COO^{-}  (weak, basicity = 1)
H_{2}SO_{4} → 2H^{+} + SO_{4}^{2-}  (dibasic, basicity = 2)
steps.narration: Strong acids and bases ionise almost completely in water, giving many mobile ions and high conductivity. Weak ones ionise only slightly. Basicity counts only ionisable hydrogen ions per acid molecule, so ethanoic acid is monobasic.

steps.title: The pH and pOH scales
working: 10^{-3} mol/dm^{3} HCl → pH = 3;   10^{-3} mol/dm^{3} NaOH → pOH = 3, pH = 11
steps.narration: At twenty five degrees Celsius, p H equals minus log base ten of hydroxonium concentration, p O H equals minus log base ten of hydroxide concentration, and p H plus p O H equals fourteen. Lower p H means stronger acidity.

steps.title: Neutralisation and indicators
working: Strong acid + strong base → any indicator (pH jump 4 to 10)
Strong acid + weak base (e.g. Na_{2}CO_{3}) → methyl orange (red acid, yellow alkali)
Weak acid + strong base → phenolphthalein (colourless acid, pink alkali)
steps.narration: Neutralisation combines hydrogen ions from an acid with hydroxide ions from a base to form water and a salt. Pick an indicator whose colour change matches the equivalence p H, methyl orange for weak bases and phenolphthalein for weak acids.

steps.title: Concentration and titration ratio
steps.display: \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}}     and     Conc (g/dm^{3}) = Conc (mol/dm^{3}) × Molar mass
working: Dilution: C_{1} V_{1} = C_{2} V_{2}  (moles stay constant)
steps.narration: Molar concentration is moles per decimetre cubed, while mass concentration in grams per decimetre cubed equals molar concentration times molar mass. In titration, always write the balanced equation first so your mole ratio matches the stoichiometry.

steps.title: Types of salts and hydrolysis
steps.display: Salts: normal (NaCl), acid (NaHSO_{4}), basic (Zn(OH)Cl), double (KAl(SO_{4})_{2}·12H_{2}O)
working: Strong acid + strong base (NaCl) → neutral (pH = 7)
Strong acid + weak base (NH_{4}Cl) → acidic (NH_{4}^{+} + H_{2}O ⇌ NH_{3} + H_{3}O^{+})
Weak acid + strong base (Na_{2}CO_{3}) → alkaline (CO_{3}^{2-} + H_{2}O ⇌ HCO_{3}^{-} + OH^{-})
Insoluble salts (AgCl, BaSO_{4}) → prepared by double decomposition
steps.narration: Normal salts replace all acidic hydrogens, acid salts keep replaceable hydrogen, basic salts keep hydroxide, and double salts combine two simple salts. In water, salts of weak bases hydrolyse to acidic solutions, while salts of weak acids hydrolyse to alkaline solutions.

steps.title: Read the mass, volume, and goal
steps.display: Find the pH at 25 °C of 0.80 g NaOH in 200 cm^{3} solution. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
working: Goal: find pH via concentration and pOH
steps.narration: Let us connect mass concentration, molar concentration, and p H in one clean problem. We have zero point eight zero grams of sodium hydroxide in two hundred centimetres cubed of solution at twenty five degrees Celsius.

steps.title: Find g/dm^{3} and mol/dm^{3}
working: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol
Molar conc = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.10 mol/dm^{3} = 10^{-1} mol/dm^{3}
steps.narration: First convert two hundred centimetres cubed to zero point two zero zero decimetres cubed, giving four point zero grams per decimetre cubed. Divide by forty grams per mole to get zero point one zero moles per decimetre cubed.

steps.title: Use strong-base dissociation
steps.narration: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali that dissociates completely, so hydroxide ion concentration equals ten to the power minus one moles per decimetre cubed. Taking minus log base ten gives p O H equal to one.

steps.title: Convert pOH to pH
working: Check: pH 13 > 7, strongly alkaline as expected for NaOH
steps.narration: Since p H plus p O H equals fourteen at twenty five degrees Celsius, subtract one from fourteen to obtain p H thirteen. That strongly alkaline value makes full sense for sodium hydroxide.

steps.title: Read the titration question
steps.display: A 15.00 cm^{3} sample of H_{2}SO_{4} neutralizes 25.00 cm^{3} of 0.125 mol/dm^{3} NaOH. Find [H_{2}SO_{4}].
steps.narration: Here is a real JAMB titration question. Fifteen point zero zero centimetres cubed of tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, sulfuric acid, neutralises twenty five point zero zero centimetres cubed of zero point one two five moles per decimetre cubed sodium hydroxide.

steps.title: Balance the equation first
working: n_{A} = 1 mol H_{2}SO_{4},   n_{B} = 2 mol NaOH
Acid-to-base mole ratio = 1 : 2
steps.narration: Always write the balanced equation before substituting numbers. One mole of dibasic tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, sulfuric acid, neutralises two moles of sodium hydroxide, so the acid to base mole ratio is one to two.

steps.title: Apply the titration formula
working: Volumes V_{A} and V_{B} are both in cm^{3}, so units cancel
steps.narration: Substitute into the titration formula with both volumes in centimetres cubed. Acid concentration times fifteen point zero zero, divided by zero point one two five times twenty five point zero zero, equals one over two.

steps.title: Calculate the acid concentration
steps.narration: Multiplying zero point one two five by twenty five gives three point one two five, and dividing by thirty gives zero point one zero four moles per decimetre cubed. Checking with actual moles confirms the exact same answer.

steps.title: Do not assume a 1 : 1 ratio or count all H atoms
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{1}{1} for H_{2}SO_{4}   |   Right: \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}} = \frac{1}{2}
working: H_{2}SO_{4} is dibasic (n_{A} = 1 reacts with 2 NaOH)
CH_{3}COOH has 4 H atoms, but only 1 ionisable H^{+} (basicity = 1)
steps.narration: Many JAMB traps assume one to one stoichiometry for dibasic acids or count non-acidic methyl hydrogens in ethanoic acid. Always check the balanced neutralisation equation and count only ionisable protons.

steps.title: Do not report pOH as the pH of an alkali
steps.display: 0.001 mol/dm^{3} NaOH:   Wrong: pH = 3   |   Right: pOH = 3 → pH = 14 - 3 = 11
working: NaOH and KOH furnish OH^{-}, not H_{3}O^{+}
Always subtract pOH from 14 for alkalis at 25 °C
steps.narration: When given sodium or potassium hydroxide at zero point zero zero one moles per decimetre cubed, minus log gives three, which is p O H, not p H. Subtract from fourteen to get p H eleven.

steps.title: Do not assume every salt is neutral
steps.display: Wrong: all salts have pH = 7   |   Right: check hydrolysis and acid salts
working: KHSO_{4}(aq): acidic (acid salt donates H^{+})
steps.narration: Not every salt forms a neutral solution. Sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) hydrolyses to give an alkaline solution, ammonium chloride hydrolyses to give an acidic solution, and potassium hydrogentetraoxosulphate(VI) is an acid salt that turns litmus red.

steps.title: One rule to carry into the exam
steps.display: Count real ions: H_{3}O^{+} vs OH^{-}, balanced mole ratios, and salt hydrolysis.
working: pH + pOH = 14   |   \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}}   |   Check weak-ion hydrolysis
steps.narration: Track the ions actually in water, use p H plus p O H equals fourteen for alkalis, balance every titration ratio first, and check salt hydrolysis before predicting litmus colour.

quickCheck.stem: What is the pH of 0.001 mol/dm^{3} NaOH at 25°C, assuming complete dissociation?

options.why: A pH of 14 corresponds in this model to 1 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
A pH of 13 corresponds to 0.1 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
A pH of 12 corresponds to 0.01 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
The OH^{-} concentration is 10^{-3} mol/dm^{3}, so pOH = 3. At 25°C, pH = 14 − 3 = 11.

steps.title: A hand-to-hand money swap
steps.display: Giver loses cash (oxidised)  →  Receiver gains cash (reduced)
working: No one can gain unless another gives
Oxidation and reduction always happen together
steps.narration: When you hand cash to a friend at the market, your wallet drops while theirs rises. In redox reactions, electrons move the same way, so loss and gain happen together.

steps.title: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers
steps.display: Free element = 0   |   Monatomic ion = charge   |   Sum = 0 (molecule) or ion charge
working: Oxygen = -2 (except peroxides like H_{2}O_{2}: -1; OF_{2}: +2)
Hydrogen = +1 (except metal hydrides like NaH, NaBH_{4}: -1)
Group I metals = +1,  Group II = +2,  Group III = +3
steps.narration: Free elements have oxidation number zero, and monatomic ions equal their charge. Oxygen is usually minus two except minus one in peroxides, while hydrogen is plus one except minus one in metal hydrides. All oxidation numbers sum to the total charge.

steps.title: Oxidation vs reduction
steps.display: Oxidation: e^{-} loss (O.N. ↑)     |     Reduction: e^{-} gain (O.N. ↓)
working: Zn(s) → Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}   (O.N. 0 → +2, oxidation)
Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-} → Cu(s)   (O.N. +2 → 0, reduction)
Also classically: +O or -H is oxidation; -O or +H is reduction
steps.narration: Remember oil rig. Oxidation is loss of electrons, which makes oxidation number go up. Reduction is gain of electrons, which makes oxidation number go down. Adding oxygen or removing hydrogen also corresponds to oxidation.

steps.title: Oxidising and reducing agents
steps.display: Oxidising agent accepts e^{-} (is reduced)   |   Reducing agent donates e^{-} (is oxidised)
working: Acidified KMnO_{4} (purple MnO_{4}^{-}) → colourless Mn^{2+} (test for reducing agent)
Acidified K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7} (orange Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}) → green Cr^{3+} (test for reducing agent)
Common reductants: Fe^{2+}, I^{-}, H_{2}S, C, CO, NaBH_{4}
Disproportionation: same species both oxidised and reduced (e.g. KClO_{3})
steps.narration: An oxidising agent takes electrons and gets reduced itself, while a reducing agent gives electrons and gets oxidised. Purple acidified potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII), potassium permanganate, turns colourless, and orange acidified dichromate turns green when mixed with a reducing agent.

steps.title: Balancing simple redox equations
steps.display: Balance atoms (O with H_{2}O, H with H^{+}), balance charge with e^{-}, equalise e^{-}
working: 1. Split into oxidation and reduction half-equations
2. Balance non-H/O atoms, then O using H_{2}O, then H using H^{+} (acid)
3. Add e^{-} to balance charge on each half
4. Multiply halves so e^{-} lost = e^{-} gained, add and cancel
steps.narration: To balance a redox equation in acidic solution, split it into oxidation and reduction halves. Balance other atoms first, add water for oxygen, add hydrogen ions for hydrogen, add electrons for charge, then multiply so electrons cancel cleanly.

steps.title: Assign oxidation numbers to each half
steps.display: Balance in acid:   Fe^{2+} + MnO_{4}^{-} → Fe^{3+} + Mn^{2+}
working: Oxidation half: Fe^{2+} (+2) → Fe^{3+} (+3)
Reduction half: Mn in MnO_{4}^{-} is +7 (x + 4(-2) = -1) → Mn^{2+} (+2)
steps.narration: Let us balance iron two plus plus tetraoxomanganate(VII), permanganate, in acidic medium. Iron rises from plus two to plus three, which is oxidation, while manganese drops from plus seven to plus two, which is reduction.

steps.title: Balance O, H, and charge for permanganate
working: Balance O with 4H_{2}O on right; balance H with 8H^{+} on left
Left charge before e^{-}: -1 + 8(+1) = +7; right = +2 → add 5e^{-} on left
steps.narration: Four oxygens on the left need four water molecules on the right, and eight hydrogens need eight hydrogen ions on the left. Adding five electrons to the left balances the charge at plus two on both sides.

steps.title: Scale the iron half-equation
working: Each Fe^{2+} loses 1e^{-}; MnO_{4}^{-} gains 5e^{-}
Multiply the iron half by 5 so electrons lost = 5
steps.narration: Each iron two plus ion loses only one electron, whereas each tetraoxomanganate(VII) ion gains five. Multiply the entire iron half equation by five so both halves exchange five electrons.

steps.title: Add halves and verify atoms and charge
working: Atoms: 5 Fe, 1 Mn, 4 O, 8 H on both sides
steps.narration: Add the two half equations and cancel the five electrons. Every element matches, and total charge is plus seventeen on both the left and right sides.

steps.title: Read the past question
steps.display: In H_{2}O(g) + C(s) → H_{2}(g) + CO(g), which reactant acts as the oxidizing agent?
working: Options: CO(g), C(s), H_{2}O(g), H_{2}(g)
Note: an oxidising agent must be a reactant, not a product
steps.narration: Here is a real JAMB question. When steam reacts with solid carbon to form hydrogen gas and carbon monoxide, we want the reactant that acts as the oxidising agent.

steps.title: Find the oxidation number of every atom
working: Reactants: H = +1, O = -2 in H_{2}O;  C = 0 (free element)
Products: H = 0 in H_{2};  C = +2, O = -2 in CO
steps.narration: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom. In steam, hydrogen is plus one and oxygen is minus two, while free carbon is zero. On the right, hydrogen gas is zero and carbon in carbon monoxide is plus two.

steps.title: Identify which species is reduced
steps.display: C: 0 → +2 (oxidised)     |     H in H_{2}O: +1 → 0 (reduced)
working: C increases 0 → +2, so C(s) is oxidised (reducing agent)
H in H_{2}O decreases +1 → 0, so H_{2}O(g) is reduced
steps.narration: Carbon rises from zero to plus two, meaning carbon is oxidised and serves as the reducing agent. Hydrogen in steam drops from plus one to zero, meaning steam itself is reduced.

steps.title: Pick the oxidising agent
steps.display: Oxidising agent = H_{2}O(g)  (the reactant that gets reduced)
working: CO(g) and H_{2}(g) are products, not reactants
C(s) is oxidised (reductant); H_{2}O(g) is reduced (oxidant)
steps.narration: Because the oxidising agent is the reactant that undergoes reduction, steam is the oxidising agent. Carbon monoxide and hydrogen gas are products, while solid carbon is the reducing agent.

steps.title: Do not treat hydride H as +1 or flip the sign
working: In metal hydrides (NaH, NaBH_{4}), H is -1 (more electronegative than metal/B)
In NH_{3}: x + 3(+1) = 0 ⇒ N = -3 (do not forget to flip sign from +3)
steps.narration: In metal hydrides like sodium borohydride, hydrogen takes minus one, giving boron plus three, not minus one which is the whole ion charge. Also in ammonia, solve x plus three equals zero carefully so nitrogen is minus three, not plus three.

steps.title: Do not pick a product or reverse oxidant vs reductant
steps.display: Wrong: oxidising agent = species oxidised (or a product)   |   Right: reactant that is reduced
working: Fe^{3+} + I^{-} → Fe^{2+} + \frac{1}{2}I_{2}:  I^{-} is oxidised → reducing agent
I_{2} and Fe^{2+} are products, never agents in the forward reaction
steps.narration: Students often call the oxidised species the oxidising agent, or pick a product like iodine or iron two plus. Remember the agents are always reactants, and the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced.

steps.title: Do not confuse dichromate(VI) with permanganate(VII) or ion charge
working: Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} (heptaoxodichromate(VI)): two Cr atoms share +12 → +6 each
MnO_{4}^{-} (tetraoxomanganate(VII)): x + 4(-2) = -1 → Mn = +7
steps.narration: Do not confuse orange dichromate with purple tetraoxomanganate(VII), and never report the minus two ion charge as chromium's state. Divide by the subscript two in dichromate to find chromium is plus six, while manganese in permanganate is plus seven.

steps.title: One rule to carry into the exam
steps.display: O.N. ↑ = oxidation (reducing agent)  |  O.N. ↓ = reduction (oxidising agent)
working: Assign every oxidation number first, then balance atoms, electrons, and charge
steps.narration: Assign every oxidation number carefully with the peroxide and hydride exceptions, match rising numbers to the reducing agent and falling numbers to the oxidising agent, and balance electrons and charge.

quickCheck.stem: What is the oxidation state of chromium in K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}?

options.why: +7 would make the sum +2 rather than zero.
+5 would make the sum −2.
+4 would make the sum −4.

steps.title: Plating a Spoon with Silver
steps.display: DC power → mobile ions move → new substance forms
working: Battery pushes electrons into the cathode (−)
Dissolved silver ions coat the spoon evenly
steps.narration: Think of plating a brass spoon with silver. A battery pushes dissolved metal ions through liquid onto the spoon, driving a non-spontaneous chemical change.

steps.title: Electrolytes and Electrodes
steps.display: Anode (+): oxidation | Cathode (−): reduction
working: Electrolytes: mobile ions (molten or aqueous)
Non-electrolytes: neutral molecules only (sugar, ethanol)
Cations (+) → Cathode (−) (gain e^{-})
Anions (−) → Anode (+) (lose e^{-})
steps.narration: Electrolytes conduct electricity via mobile ions when molten or dissolved, while non-electrolytes like ethanol do not. Remember CRAO, cathode reduction and anode oxidation. Positive cations gain electrons at the cathode, while negative anions lose electrons at the anode.

steps.title: Preferential Discharge of Ions
steps.display: Lower ion in series discharges first (unless high halide concentration or active anode)
working: 2. Concentration effect favours halide anions (Cl^{-}, Br^{-}, I^{-})
3. Active anode (Cu, Ag) dissolves instead of discharging anions
4. Mercury cathode discharges Na^{+} preferentially over H^{+}
steps.narration: In aqueous solutions, water supplies hydrogen and hydroxide ions alongside salt ions. Three factors decide which ion discharges first, position in the electrochemical series, high concentration for halide anions only, and whether the electrode itself is inert or active.

steps.title: Products at Each Electrode
steps.display: Molten: 2 ions only | Aqueous: compare H^{+}/OH^{-} and electrode
working: Molten PbBr_{2}: Pb at cathode, Br_{2} at anode
Dilute H_{2}SO_{4} (Pt): 2 vol H_{2} (cathode), 1 vol O_{2} (anode)
Brine, conc. NaCl (C): H_{2} (cathode), Cl_{2} (anode), NaOH left
CuSO_{4}(aq): Cu (cathode); O_{2} (Pt anode) or Cu^{2+} (Cu anode)
steps.narration: Molten lead two bromide yields lead and bromine directly. With inert electrodes, dilute tetraoxosulphate six acid, sulphuric acid, gives hydrogen and oxygen, while brine gives hydrogen, chlorine and alkaline sodium hydroxide. A copper anode dissolves to refine or electroplate copper.

steps.title: Faraday's First Law and Q = It
steps.display: Q = It,   n(e^{-}) = \frac{Q}{F},   m = \frac{ItM}{cF}
working: Q in C, I in A, t in s (1 F = 96,500 C/mol e^{-})
M^{c+} + ce^{-} → M needs c moles of e^{-} per mole M
n(M) = \frac{n(e^{-})}{c} = \frac{It}{cF}
STP gas volume = n(gas) × 22.4 dm^{3}/mol
steps.narration: Faraday's first law states that mass deposited is proportional to charge passed, where charge equals current times time in seconds. Divide charge by ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole to get electron moles, then divide by the ion charge.

steps.title: Faraday's Second Law (Cells in Series)
steps.display: n_{1}c_{1} = n_{2}c_{2}   or   \left(\frac{m}{M}\right)_{1}c_{1} = \left(\frac{m}{M}\right)_{2}c_{2}
working: Same Q in series → same moles of electrons
Moles deposited n ∝ \frac{1}{c} (inverse of ion charge)
1 F deposits 1 mol Ag^{+}, \frac{1}{2} mol Cu^{2+}, \frac{1}{3} mol Al^{3+}
steps.narration: Faraday's second law states that for electrolytes in series carrying the same charge, moles deposited vary inversely with ion charge. One faraday deposits one mole of silver, half a mole of copper two plus, or one third mole of aluminium.

steps.title: Convert Time and Find Charge Q
steps.display: I = 2.0 A, t = 16 min 5 s → Q = It
steps.narration: First convert time completely to seconds because amperes times seconds gives coulombs. Sixteen minutes times sixty plus five gives nine hundred and sixty five seconds. Multiplying by two amperes gives one thousand nine hundred and thirty coulombs.

steps.title: Convert Charge to Moles of Electrons
steps.narration: Next divide the total charge in coulombs by the Faraday constant, ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole. That gives zero point zero two zero moles of electrons flowing through the cell.

steps.title: Use Half-Equation to Find Mass of Copper
working: 2 mol e^{-} deposit 1 mol Cu
steps.narration: Each copper two plus ion takes two electrons at the cathode, so divide electron moles by two to get zero point zero one mole of copper. Multiply by sixty four grams per mole to obtain zero point six four grams.

steps.title: Read the Past Question and Find Charge
steps.display: A current of 5 A flows for 193 s through acidified water. What volume of oxygen forms at STP? Use 96,500 C/mol of electrons and 22.4 dm^{3} per mole of gas.
working: Time is already in seconds: t = 193 s
steps.narration: In this JAMB twenty thirteen question, time is already in seconds, so multiply five amperes by one hundred and ninety three seconds. That gives nine hundred and sixty five coulombs of electricity passing through the acidified water.

steps.title: Find Moles of Electrons
working: 1 mol e^{-} carries 96,500 C
steps.narration: Divide nine hundred and sixty five coulombs by ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole. Notice how cleanly those numbers cancel to give zero point zero one zero mole of electrons.

steps.title: Apply the Anode Half-Equation for Oxygen
working: 4 mol e^{-} liberate 1 mol O_{2}
steps.narration: At the inert anode, hydroxide ions discharge preferentially over tetraoxosulphate six ions. Four electrons are released for every one oxygen molecule formed. Therefore divide zero point zero one zero mole of electrons by four to get zero point zero zero two five mole of oxygen.

steps.title: Convert Moles of Oxygen to Volume at STP
working: At STP, 1 mol gas occupies 22.4 dm^{3}
steps.narration: Multiply zero point zero zero two five mole by twenty two point four cubic decimetres per mole. That gives zero point zero five six cubic decimetres, matching the correct answer rather than fifty six cubic centimetres mislabelled in cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Forgetting Ion Charge or Electron Count
steps.display: Wrong: n(metal) = n(e^{-})  |  Right: n = \frac{n(e^{-})}{c}
working: Al^{3+} + 3e^{-} → Al: divide by 3, not 1
steps.narration: Students often multiply electron moles straight by molar mass and forget ion charge. Aluminium three plus needs three electrons per atom, and one oxygen molecule needs four electrons. Always write the balanced half-equation first so you divide by the exact electron count.

steps.title: Ignoring Preferential Discharge or Electrode Role
steps.display: Wrong: Na deposits from NaCl(aq)  |  Right: H_{2} forms at cathode
working: In water, H^{+} discharges before Na^{+}; OH^{-} beats SO_{4}^{2-}
Electroplating: object is cathode (−), plating metal is anode (+)
steps.narration: Never assume dissolved sodium or potassium salts deposit metal at an inert cathode in water, because hydrogen ions discharge first. Also remember in electroplating, connect the object to be coated as the negative cathode where reduction occurs, never the anode.

steps.title: Time and Volume Unit Slips
steps.display: Wrong: t in min, or cm^{3} as dm^{3}  |  Right: t in s, 1 dm^{3} = 1,000 cm^{3}
working: 16 min → 16 × 60 = 960 s before Q = It
steps.narration: Two classic unit traps catch candidates in JAMB calculations. Never plug minutes or hours directly into Q equals I t, always convert time into seconds first. Also check whether gas volume options are in cubic centimetres or cubic decimetres before selecting.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Pick the winning ions at each electrode, then link charge Q = It through moles of electrons and ion charge c.
working: Cathode = reduction, Anode = oxidation, n(product) = \frac{It}{cF}
steps.narration: Pick the preferentially discharged ions at cathode and anode, then divide total charge by Faraday's constant and the half-equation electron count.

quickCheck.stem: A quantity of electricity liberates 3.6 g of silver from its salt. What mass of aluminium would the same quantity of electricity liberate from its salt? Take Al = 27 and Ag = 108.

options.why: 2.7 g is nine times the mass from the shared electron amount.
1.2 g comes from dividing the silver mass by three while ignoring the different molar masses.
0.9 g accounts for molar mass but ignores the three electrons needed per aluminium ion.

\frac{3.6}{108} mol of silver uses the same number of moles of electrons because Ag^{+} needs one each. Each Al^{3+} needs three, so aluminium mass is \left(\frac{3.6}{108}\right) × \frac{27}{3} = 0.30 g.

lessons.title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

steps.title: A Marble on a Football Pitch
steps.display: Tiny heavy nucleus (p^{+} + n^{0})  |  Wide electron shells (e^{-})
working: Centre marble = protons + neutrons (almost all mass)
Stands around pitch = fast electrons driving chemistry
steps.narration: Picture a football pitch with a marble on the centre spot. That marble holds almost all the mass, while fast electrons fill the stands and run every chemical reaction.

steps.title: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons, Z and A
working: Proton (+1, mass 1) and Neutron (0, mass 1) in nucleus
Electron (-1, mass \frac{1}{1840}) in shells outside nucleus
Neutral atom: e^{-} = p^{+}; Cation M^{q+}: e^{-} = Z - q
Anion X^{q-}: e^{-} = Z + q
steps.narration: Protons and neutrons sit inside the tiny nucleus and form the mass number A, while tiny negative electrons occupy outer shells. Atomic number Z equals the proton count and defines the element. Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons, whereas ions gain or lose electrons.

steps.title: Isotopes and Relative Atomic Mass
working: Isotopes: same Z (protons, chemistry), different A (neutrons, mass)
steps.narration: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number and electron arrangement, so identical chemistry, but different neutron numbers and masses. Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of all natural isotope masses using their percentage or ratio abundances.

steps.title: Shells and s, p, d Electron Configuration
working: Max per shell = 2n^{2}: K(2), L(8), M(18), N(32)
Subshell capacity: s(2), p(6), d(10), f(14); 2 e^{-} per orbital (Pauli)
Hund: fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing
Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d^{5}4s^{1}, Cu = [Ar] 3d^{10}4s^{1}
steps.narration: Electrons fill subshells from lowest energy up, with four s before three d. Pauli's principle limits each orbital to two opposite-spin electrons, and Hund's rule fills equal orbitals singly before pairing. Chromium and copper stabilise half-filled or filled three d subshells.

steps.title: How Configuration Sets Group, Period and Block
steps.display: Period = highest n  |  Main Group = valence e^{-} (ns + np)
working: Modern table orders by increasing atomic number Z
Mg (3s^{2}): n = 3 (Period 3), 2 valence e^{-} (Group II / 2, s-block)
Cl (3s^{2} 3p^{5}): 7 valence e^{-} (Group VII / 17, halogen, p-block)
He (1s^{2}), Ne, Ar: full outer shell (Group 0 / 18, noble gases)
steps.narration: Elements sit in order of atomic number. Highest occupied shell gives the period, while outer s plus p electrons set the main group, Roman one to seven and zero or IUPAC one to eighteen. Partly filled d subshells mark transition metals.

steps.title: Periodic Trends Across Periods and Down Groups
steps.display: Across Period (→): radius ↓, IE ↑, EA ↑, EN ↑
working: Down Group (↓): more shells, shielding ↑, radius ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓
Metallic character: decreases across period (→), increases down group (↓)
Group I reactivity ↑ down group (easier valence e^{-} loss)
Group VII reactivity ↓ down group (harder e^{-} gain)
steps.narration: Across a period, rising nuclear charge pulls the same outer shell tighter, so atomic radius shrinks while ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity rise. Down a group, extra shells increase shielding and radius, making alkali metals more reactive but halogens less reactive.

steps.title: Count Protons, Neutrons and Electrons in ^{31}_{15}P
working: Protons = Z = 15
Electrons (neutral atom) = 15
Neutrons = A - Z = 31 - 15 = 16
steps.narration: Take a neutral phosphorus atom with atomic number fifteen and mass number thirty one. Its proton count is fifteen, and because it is neutral, its electron count is also fifteen. Subtract fifteen from thirty one to get sixteen neutrons.

steps.title: Write the s, p, d Configuration and Check Hund's Rule
working: Remaining 3 electrons: 3p_{x}^{1} 3p_{y}^{1} 3p_{z}^{1}
3 unpaired electrons (Hund's rule)
steps.narration: Fill subshells in energy order until all fifteen electrons are placed. Twelve electrons fill up to three s two, leaving three electrons for the three p orbitals. By Hund's rule, those three electrons occupy separate p orbitals singly, giving three unpaired electrons.

steps.title: Deduce Period, Block and Group
steps.display: 3s^{2} 3p^{3}  →  Period 3, p-block, Group V (15)
working: Highest occupied shell n = 3 → Period 3
Valence electrons = 2 + 3 = 5 → Group V (IUPAC 15)
Outer electron enters 3p → p-block non-metal
steps.narration: Look at the outermost third shell. The highest shell number three places phosphorus in Period three, while adding the two three s and three three p electrons gives five valence electrons, placing it in Group five, or fifteen, in the p block.

steps.title: Read the Isotope Ratio Question
steps.display: Element X has two isotopes with mass numbers 20 and 22, present in the ratio 1:3. What is the relative atomic mass of X?
working: Mass numbers: A_{1} = 20,  A_{2} = 22
Ratio parts: R_{1} = 1,  R_{2} = 3
steps.narration: In this JAMB twenty sixteen question, element X has two isotopes of mass numbers twenty and twenty two in the ratio one to three. That means out of every four atoms, one has mass twenty and three have mass twenty two.

steps.title: Sum the Weighted Contributions
working: Lighter isotope contribution: 20 × 1 = 20
Heavier isotope contribution: 22 × 3 = 66
Total ratio parts: 1 + 3 = 4
steps.narration: Multiply each isotopic mass by its ratio share. One times twenty gives twenty, and three times twenty two gives sixty six, making eighty six in total across one plus three equals four parts.

steps.title: Divide by Total Parts to Get A_{r}
working: Closer to 22 than 20 because ratio favours 22
steps.narration: Divide eighty six by four to get twenty one point five. Always check that your answer leans towards the more abundant isotope. Here seventy five percent is mass twenty two, so twenty one point five makes complete sense rather than the plain average twenty one.

steps.title: Counting Only p Electrons as Valence Electrons
steps.display: Wrong: 3s^{2} 3p^{5} has 5 valence e^{-}  |  Right: 2 + 5 = 7 valence e^{-}
working: Valence shell = ALL electrons in highest n (both ns and np)
1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{5}: 7 outer electrons → Group VII (17)
steps.narration: Many candidates read the last subshell alone and think three s two three p five has five valence electrons. You must add all electrons in the highest shell, both three s and three p, giving seven valence electrons and placing it with the halogens.

steps.title: Mixing Up Nucleons, Mass Number and Electrons
steps.display: Wrong: n^{0} = A, or e^{-} in nucleus  |  Right: n^{0} = A - Z
working: Nucleus contains ONLY protons and neutrons (nucleons)
Tritium ^{3}_{1}H: 1 proton, 3 - 1 = 2 neutrons (no e^{-} inside)
steps.narration: Do not confuse mass number with neutron count, and never place electrons inside the nucleus. Only protons and neutrons live in the nucleus. For tritium, subtract atomic number one from mass number three to get two neutrons alongside one proton.

steps.title: Unweighted Isotope Averages and Period Radius Traps
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{20+22}{2} = 21.0; radius ↑ across period
working: Right: weight each isotope by its abundance or ratio
Right: across a period (→), higher nuclear charge shrinks atomic radius
steps.narration: Two frequent JAMB traps appear in isotopes and trends. Never average isotope masses without weighting by abundance or ratio. Also remember that moving left to right across a period adds protons to the same shell, pulling electrons closer so atomic radius decreases.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Protons fix identity and isotopes give weighted mass, while outer s and p electrons govern group, period and periodic trends.
working: Z = p^{+}, A_{r} = weighted mean, Period = max n, Group = valence e^{-}
steps.narration: Proton number defines the element, weighted isotopes give relative atomic mass, and outer electron configuration explains every periodic group, period and trend.

quickCheck.stem: Which statement is true of an atom with configuration 1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{5}?

options.text: Its outer p subshell is full
options.why: The outer 3p subshell can hold six electrons and has only five.

options.text: It has five electrons in its outer shell
options.why: The outer shell contains two 3s electrons as well as five 3p electrons.
Group 2 atoms normally have two valence electrons.
The valence configuration 3s^{2} 3p^{5} has seven electrons, characteristic of Group 17. This atom is chlorine, a halogen.

steps.title: Handing Over, Sharing, or Pooling Together
steps.display: Transfer (ionic)  |  Equal share (covalent)  |  One gives both (dative)  |  Shared sea (metallic)
working: Ionic: one hands over, one receives
Covalent: both contribute equally to share
Dative: one friend pays for both
steps.narration: Think of sharing suya with a friend. Either you split the bill, one person pays for both, or one hands over cash completely. Atoms bond in similar ways.

steps.title: Ionic (Electrovalent) Bonding
steps.display: Metal (low IE) + Non-metal (high EA)  →  M^{m+} + X^{x-}  →  M_{x}X_{m}
working: Large electronegativity difference favours electron transfer
Non-directional electrostatic attraction builds a giant crystal lattice
steps.narration: Ionic or electrovalent bonding happens when atoms with widely different electronegativities transfer valence electrons, usually a metal losing electrons to a non-metal. Opposite ions attract in every direction to build a crystal lattice. Ions combine in the inverse ratio of their charges.

steps.title: Covalent and Dative (Coordinate) Bonding
steps.display: Covalent: A· + ·B → A:B   |   Dative: A: + B → A→B
working: Single (H-H), double (O=O), triple (N≡N) shared electron pairs
Non-polar (H_{2}, Cl_{2}: equal EN) vs polar (H-Cl, H_{2}O: unequal EN)
Dative: donor lone pair + acceptor empty orbital (NH_{3} + H^{+} → NH_{4}^{+})
Once formed, a dative bond behaves identically to a covalent bond
steps.narration: In ordinary covalent bonding, two non-metals each contribute one electron to share a pair, forming discrete molecules with single, double or triple bonds. In dative or coordinate bonding, one donor atom supplies both electrons of the shared pair into an empty orbital.

steps.title: Metallic Bonding
steps.display: Positive metal ions  ↔  mobile sea of delocalised valence e^{-}
working: Metals have low ionisation energies and vacant valence orbitals
Mobile electrons carry electric current and thermal energy
Non-directional bonding allows ion layers to slip without shattering
Explains lustre, malleability, ductility and high melting points
steps.narration: Metallic bonding holds positive metal ions inside a mobile sea of delocalised valence electrons. Because electrons move freely throughout the lattice, metals conduct electricity and heat well. Because the attraction is non-directional, hammered layers can slip past each other without snapping.

steps.title: Van der Waals Forces and Hydrogen Bonds
steps.display: Dispersion (weakest) < Dipole-dipole < Hydrogen bond (F, O, N) << Covalent
working: Van der Waals dispersion: acts between all molecules (holds I_{2}, Ar, CH_{4})
Dipole-dipole: aligns permanent dipoles in polar molecules (HCl)
Hydrogen bond: H bonded to F, O or N attracts lone pair on nearby F, O or N
H-bonding raises b.p. of H_{2}O, HF, NH_{3}, alkanols; makes ice open and less dense
steps.narration: Weak intermolecular forces act between separate molecules. Van der Waals dispersion forces increase with molar mass and hold non-polar molecules like iodine together. Hydrogen bonds form when hydrogen joins fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, raising water's boiling point and giving ice an open lattice.

steps.title: Shapes of Simple Molecules (VSEPR)
steps.display: Electron pairs repel → maximum separation around central atom
working: 2 BP, 0 LP → linear, 180° (CO_{2}, BeCl_{2}, C_{2}H_{2}); 3 BP, 0 LP → trigonal planar, 120° (BF_{3})
4 BP, 0 LP → tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH_{4}, NH_{4}^{+})
3 BP, 1 LP → trigonal pyramidal, 107° (NH_{3}); 2 BP, 2 LP → bent or V-shape, 105° (H_{2}O)
Symmetrical shapes (CO_{2}, CH_{4}, CCl_{4}) cancel bond dipoles → non-polar molecule
steps.narration: By electron-pair repulsion, bond pairs and lone pairs arrange as far apart as possible, with lone pairs repelling more strongly and shrinking bond angles. Two pairs give linear shapes, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal, and water bent. Symmetrical shapes cancel dipoles.

steps.title: Properties That Follow from Bonding
steps.display: Structure + Bond Type  →  Melting point, Solubility, Conductivity, Hardness
working: Ionic crystals: high m.p., brittle, soluble in water, conduct when molten or aqueous
Simple molecular: low m.p./b.p., soft, non-conductors (unless ionised in water)
Giant covalent: diamond (3D, non-conductor) vs graphite (2D layers, conducts)
Polar water dissolves ions (ion-dipole) and H-bonding molecules (like dissolves like)
steps.narration: Bonding governs bulk behaviour. Ionic solids melt high, shatter when shifted, and conduct only when molten or dissolved so ions can move. Simple molecular solids melt low and never conduct. Giant networks melt very high, while graphite conducts along layers via delocalised electrons.

steps.title: Classify Potassium Chloride and Water
steps.display: Compare KCl (_{19}K + _{17}Cl) and H_{2}O (_{1}H + _{8}O)
working: _{19}K (2,8,8,1): Group I metal;  _{17}Cl (2,8,7): Group VII non-metal
_{1}H (1) and _{8}O (2,6): both non-metals
steps.narration: First inspect the elements in potassium chloride and water. Potassium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a non-metal, whereas hydrogen and oxygen are both non-metals. That contrast immediately separates electron transfer from electron sharing.

steps.title: Assign Bond Types and Shape
steps.display: KCl: K^{+}Cl^{-} (ionic)   |   H_{2}O: bent (105°), polar + H-bonds
working: K loses 1 e^{-} → K^{+}; Cl gains 1 e^{-} → Cl^{-} (electrostatic lattice)
O shares 2 pairs with H (2 BP, 2 LP) → V-shape (105°), polar molecule
O-H groups form intermolecular hydrogen bonds between H_{2}O molecules
steps.narration: Potassium transfers one valence electron to chlorine, building an ionic crystal of potassium and chloride ions. Oxygen shares two electron pairs with hydrogen while keeping two lone pairs, giving water a bent shape and strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

steps.title: Predict Melting, Solubility and Conductivity
steps.display: KCl: high-m.p. solid, conducts molten/aq   |   H_{2}O: liquid, dissolves KCl
working: KCl solid: ions locked in lattice → non-conductor; molten/aq: mobile ions → conducts
H_{2}O: liquid at room temp (H-bonds); polar molecules hydrate K^{+} and Cl^{-}
steps.narration: Potassium chloride is a high-melting brittle solid that conducts electricity only when melted or dissolved, because mobile ions carry charge. Water stays liquid at room temperature due to hydrogen bonding, and its polar molecules hydrate and dissolve potassium chloride.

steps.title: Read the Ammonium Chloride Bonding Question
steps.display: Which bond types are needed in the textbook account of crystalline NH_{4}Cl, including how NH_{4}^{+} forms from NH_{3} and H^{+}?
working: Choices: (a) Ionic and covalent   (b) Ionic and coordinate
(c) Ionic, covalent and coordinate   (d) Covalent, coordinate and metallic
steps.narration: In this JAMB twenty fifteen question, we must identify every bond type present in solid ammonium chloride, N H four C l, including how ammonia combines with a hydrogen ion to form the ammonium ion.

steps.title: Check the Bonds Inside Ammonia (NH_{3})
steps.display: N (2,5) + 3 H (1)  →  3 ordinary covalent N-H bonds + 1 lone pair
working: Each H contributes 1 e^{-}; N contributes 1 e^{-} per bond (3 shared pairs)
Rule out any choice missing ordinary covalent bonds
steps.narration: Start inside the ammonia molecule, N H three. Nitrogen shares one electron with each of three hydrogen atoms to form three ordinary covalent bonds, leaving one unshared lone pair on nitrogen. Any answer that leaves out ordinary covalent bonding is incomplete.

steps.title: Trace Formation of Ammonium Ion (NH_{4}^{+})
steps.display: H_{3}N: + H^{+}  →  [NH_{4}]^{+}   (dative / coordinate covalent bond)
working: H^{+} has an empty 1s orbital and brings zero electrons
N donates both electrons of its lone pair → coordinate bond
Rule out any choice missing coordinate bonding
steps.narration: Next add the hydrogen ion, H plus, which has an empty orbital. Nitrogen donates its entire lone pair to share with H plus, forming a dative or coordinate covalent bond. That eliminates any choice that omits coordinate bonding.

steps.title: Check Crystal Packing and Rule Out Metallic Bonding
steps.display: NH_{4}^{+} + Cl^{-}  →  NH_{4}^{+}Cl^{-} (ionic lattice, no metal)
working: Oppositely charged NH_{4}^{+} and Cl^{-} ions attract electrostatically (ionic)
No metal atoms or delocalised electron sea → eliminate metallic
steps.narration: Finally pack the positive ammonium ions with negative chloride ions to build the salt crystal. Opposite ions attract via ionic bonding, and there are no metal atoms or electron seas, which rules out metallic bonding and leaves ionic, covalent and coordinate.

steps.title: Boiling Overcomes Intermolecular Forces, Not Covalent Bonds
steps.display: Wrong: boiling H_{2}O or I_{2} breaks covalent bonds (or H-bonds in I_{2})
working: Right: boiling H_{2}O/alkanols breaks intermolecular H-bonds; O-H bonds stay intact
Right: I_{2} has no H atom → molecular lattice held by van der Waals forces
Right: ice floats because H-bonds hold H_{2}O molecules in an open lattice
steps.narration: Do not confuse strong covalent bonds inside molecules with weak attractions between them. Boiling water or an alkanol breaks intermolecular hydrogen bonds, never internal covalent bonds. Iodine contains no hydrogen, so its lattice is held purely by van der Waals forces.

steps.title: Why Ionic Crystals Shatter While Metals Bend
steps.display: Wrong: shifting salt layers bends it; solid NaCl conducts current
working: Right: shifting ionic layers aligns like charges (+ near +) → repulsion → fracture
Right: ionic compounds conduct only when molten or aqueous (mobile ions)
Right: metal layers slip inside non-directional electron sea → malleable
steps.narration: Both salts and metals form lattices, yet behave oppositely under a hammer. Shifting an ionic crystal brings like charges beside each other so repulsion shatters it, and ions stay locked when solid. Metal layers slip freely within their delocalised electron sea.

steps.title: Flat Paper Drawings Hide 3D Shapes and Dipole Cancellation
steps.display: Wrong: CH_{4} is flat 90°; CO_{2} is polar because C=O is polar
working: Right: CH_{4} has 4 equal C-H bond pairs → 3D tetrahedral (109.5°)
Right: CO_{2} is linear (180°) → equal opposite C=O dipoles cancel (non-polar)
steps.narration: Drawing methane flat on paper can trick you into thinking its bond angles are ninety degrees or trigonal planar. Four electron pairs repel into a three-dimensional tetrahedron. Likewise, linear carbon dioxide cancels its two opposite bond dipoles, making the whole molecule non-polar.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Electron transfer, sharing or pooling builds the bond; 3D electron repulsion sets shape; lattice or intermolecular forces explain properties.
working: Intramolecular (ionic, covalent, dative, metallic) vs intermolecular (van der Waals, H-bond)
steps.narration: How valence electrons are transferred, shared or pooled sets the primary bond, electron-pair repulsion sets molecular shape, and the forces between particles explain melting point, solubility and conductivity.

quickCheck.stem: The molecular lattice of iodine is held together by

options.why: A coordinate bond involves a donated electron pair. The question asks what holds distinct molecules together.
Metallic bonding requires delocalised electrons in a metal lattice.
I_{2} contains no hydrogen and does not form hydrogen bonds.
Iodine forms discrete I_{2} molecules. Its molecular crystal is held together by London dispersion forces, a type of van der Waals attraction.

steps.title: Giving a Molecule a Clear Street Address
steps.display: Longest carbon road (root) + closest landmark (number) + family surname (suffix)
working: Main road = longest continuous carbon chain
House number = position closest to the functional group
Surname = family suffix (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate)
steps.narration: Naming a carbon molecule is like giving a clear street address. Find the longest main road, number from the closest landmark, and end with the family surname.

steps.title: Homologous Series and Carbon Root Names
steps.display: Consecutive homologues differ by -CH_{2}- (mass 14)   |   Root = longest chain
working: Shared general formula & functional group → similar chemical reactions
Physical properties (b.p., density) rise steadily as chain length grows
Roots: C1 meth-, C2 eth-, C3 prop-, C4 but-, C5 pent-, C6 hex-
C7 hept-, C8 oct-, C9 non-, C10 dec-; branches use -yl (CH_{3}- = methyl)
steps.narration: A homologous series is a family sharing a general formula and functional group, where each member adds one C H two unit of mass fourteen. Physical properties change gradually down the series, while the longest continuous carbon chain sets the root name.

steps.title: Functional Groups Set the Family and Suffix
steps.display: -ane (C-C)  |  -ene (C=C)  |  -yne (C≡C)  |  -ol (-OH)  |  -oic acid (-COOH)  |  -oate (-COO-)
working: Alkanes (C_{n}H_{2n+2}): single bonds only (saturated); suffix -ane
Alkenes (C_{n}H_{2n}): C=C double bond (unsaturated); suffix -ene
Alkynes (C_{n}H_{2n-2}): C≡C triple bond (unsaturated); suffix -yne
Alkanols (-OH, -ol), alkanoic acids (-COOH, -oic acid), esters (-COO-, -oate)
steps.narration: A functional group is the atom, bond or group that controls chemical reactions and gives the IUPAC suffix. Saturated alkanes end in ane, unsaturated alkenes and alkynes end in ene and yne, alkanols end in ol, acids in oic acid, and esters in oate.

steps.title: Naming Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes
steps.display: Longest chain (with C=C or C≡C) → lowest locant → alphabetical prefixes
working: Alkanes: number from end nearest first branch (CH_{3}CH(CH_{3})CH_{2}CH_{3} = 2-methylbutane)
Alkenes/alkynes: number from end nearest multiple bond (but-1-ene, but-2-yne)
Use di-, tri-, tetra- for repeated groups; commas between numbers, hyphens before letters
Alphabetise distinct substituents ignoring di-/tri- (bromo before chloro before methyl)
steps.narration: Pick the longest continuous chain containing any double or triple bond. Number from the end giving the multiple bond, or first alkane branch, the lowest number, placing that number just before ene or yne. List different substituents alphabetically with hyphens and commas.

steps.title: Naming Alkanols and Alkanoic Acids
steps.display: Alkanol: alkane - e + -ol (propan-1-ol)   |   Acid: alkane - e + -oic acid
working: Alkanols (R-OH): number chain to give -OH carbon the lowest number
Primary (RCH_{2}OH), secondary (R_{2}CHOH), tertiary (R_{3}COH, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol)
Alkanoic acids (R-COOH): -COOH carbon is ALWAYS C1 (included in chain count)
HCOOH = methanoic (formic) acid; CH_{3}COOH = ethanoic (acetic) acid
steps.narration: For alkanols, replace final e with ol and number from the end nearest the hydroxyl group, classifying the carbon holding it as primary, secondary or tertiary. For alkanoic acids, the carboxyl carbon is always carbon one, giving methanoic acid and ethanoic acid.

steps.title: Naming Esters (Alkanoates, RCOOR')
steps.display: RCOOH (acid) + R'OH (alkanol)  ⇌  RCOOR' (alkyl alkanoate) + H_{2}O
working: Two-word name: alkyl group R' (from alcohol) + acid root with -oate
R' attaches to the single-bonded oxygen (-O-R'); acid chain includes C=O carbon
HCOOCH_{3} → methyl (from CH_{3}OH) + methanoate (from HCOOH)
CH_{3}COOC_{2}H_{5} → ethyl ethanoate (familiar name: ethyl acetate)
steps.narration: Esters form when an alkanoic acid reacts with an alkanol, and carry a two-word IUPAC name. Name the alkyl group attached to the single-bonded oxygen first, then name the carbonyl-containing acid part by changing oic acid to oate, like ethyl ethanoate, ethyl acetate.

steps.title: Structural and Geometric Isomerism
steps.display: Same molecular formula, different connectivity (structural) or spatial layout (cis/trans)
working: Chain isomers: butane vs 2-methylpropane (both C_{4}H_{10})
Position isomers: propan-1-ol vs propan-2-ol (both C_{3}H_{8}O)
Functional group isomers: ethanol (CH_{3}CH_{2}OH) vs methoxymethane (CH_{3}OCH_{3})
Geometric (cis-trans): restricted C=C rotation + two different groups on EACH C=C carbon
steps.narration: Isomers share the same molecular formula but differ in structure or space. Structural isomers vary by chain branching, group position, or functional group, such as ethanol and methoxymethane. Geometric cis-trans isomers need a double bond where both carbons hold two different groups.

steps.title: Find Chain and Functional Group in CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CH_{3}
steps.display: Name CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CH_{3}   and   CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}
working: First compound: 4 carbons in continuous chain → root but-
Functional group is -OH → alkanol, suffix -ol
steps.narration: Start with the first structure. Count four carbon atoms in the continuous chain, giving the root but, and spot the hydroxyl group, which places the molecule in the alkanol family ending in ol.

steps.title: Number Closest to -OH
steps.display: CH_{3}-CH(OH)-CH_{2}-CH_{3}  →  1-2-3-4 gives -OH at C2 → butan-2-ol
working: Left to right puts -OH on carbon 2; right to left puts -OH on carbon 3
Lowest locant is 2 → butan-2-ol (a secondary alkanol)
steps.narration: Number from left to right so the hydroxyl group sits on carbon two rather than three. Combine root, position number and suffix to name it butan-two-ol, a secondary alkanol.

steps.title: Split the Ester CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}
steps.display: CH_{3}CH_{2}COO-  (3-carbon acid part)   |   -CH_{3} (1-carbon alcohol part)
working: Alkyl group on single-bonded oxygen: -CH_{3} → methyl
Acid part including carbonyl carbon: CH_{3}CH_{2}COO- (3 carbons) → propanoate
steps.narration: Now split the second compound at its ester linkage. The single-bonded oxygen holds a one-carbon methyl group from methanol, while the carbonyl side holds three carbons in total, giving the propanoate portion.

steps.title: Assemble the Two-Word Ester Name
steps.display: CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}  →  methyl propanoate
working: Alkyl part first (methyl) + acid -oate part second (propanoate)
Answers: butan-2-ol and methyl propanoate
steps.narration: Place the alkyl group before the alkanoate name to get methyl propanoate. Together, our two compounds are butan-two-ol and methyl propanoate.

steps.title: Read the Ester and Alkyne Naming Question
steps.display: What are the names of HCOOCH_{3} and HC≡CH, in that order?
working: Choices: (a) Methyl methanoate and ethene   (b) Methanoic acid and ethyne
(c) Ethyl methanoate and ethyne   (d) Methyl methanoate and ethyne
steps.narration: In this JAMB twenty fifteen question, we must name H C O O C H three and H C triple bond C H in that exact order by matching each functional group.

steps.title: Identify HCOOCH_{3} as an Ester, Not an Acid
steps.display: HCOOCH_{3} has -COO- bonded to -CH_{3} (ester), not -COOH (acid)
working: Methanoic acid would be HCOOH (ends in H, not CH_{3})
Eliminate the choice calling HCOOCH_{3} methanoic acid
steps.narration: Look closely at the first formula. Because the carboxylate oxygen connects to a methyl group instead of a hydrogen atom, it is an ester rather than methanoic acid. That removes the choice naming an acid.

steps.title: Name the Alcohol and Acid Halves of HCOOCH_{3}
steps.display: HCOO- (1 C: methanoate) + -CH_{3} (1 C: methyl)  →  methyl methanoate
working: Alcohol alkyl group is -CH_{3} (methyl), NOT -C_{2}H_{5} (ethyl)
Acid part HCOO- has 1 carbon → methanoate
Eliminate the choice giving ethyl methanoate
steps.narration: Now split the ester. The group on the single-bonded oxygen has one carbon, so it is methyl rather than ethyl, while the one-carbon carbonyl side gives methanoate. That gives methyl methanoate and rules out ethyl methanoate.

steps.title: Name HC≡CH and Confirm the Order
steps.display: HC≡CH (2 C, triple bond)  →  ethyne (acetylene), not ethene (C=C)
working: 2 carbons → eth-; triple bond (≡) → -yne → ethyne
Ethene has a double bond (CH_{2}=CH_{2}); eliminate the choice with ethene
Correct order: methyl methanoate and ethyne
steps.narration: Finally check the second formula. Two carbons joined by a triple bond belong to the alkyne family, giving ethyne, acetylene, rather than ethene which has a double bond. In order, the names are methyl methanoate and ethyne.

steps.title: Reversing the Two Halves of an Ester
steps.display: Wrong: CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3} is ethyl propanoate  |  Right: methyl propanoate
working: Alcohol alkyl group (-O-R') comes FIRST; carbonyl chain (R-COO-) gives -oate
HCOOCH_{3}: -CH_{3} (methyl) + HCOO- (methanoate), NOT ethyl or acid
steps.narration: Students often swap the two sides of an ester or overlook the carbonyl carbon when counting chain length. Always read the group attached to single-bonded oxygen as the first alkyl word, and include the carbonyl carbon inside the alkanoate chain.

steps.title: Counting Bent Chains or Different Formulas as Isomers
steps.display: Wrong: C_{4}H_{10} has 3 or 4 isomers; C_{2}H_{6}O and C_{3}H_{6}O are isomers
working: Right: isomers MUST have the exact same molecular formula
Right: bending an unbranched chain does NOT make a new isomer
C_{4}H_{10} has only 2 isomers: butane and 2-methylpropane
steps.narration: Drawing a four-carbon chain bent at a right angle does not create a third isomer of butane, because the connectivity stays unbranched. Always verify that both molecules share the exact same molecular formula before calling them isomers.

steps.title: Expecting Cis-Trans Isomerism on Terminal Alkenes
steps.display: Wrong: prop-1-ene (CH_{3}CH=CH_{2}) has cis-trans isomers
working: Right: EACH C=C carbon must carry two different groups (a ≠ b and e ≠ f)
Terminal =CH_{2} has two identical H atoms → NO cis-trans isomerism
Internal alkenes like hex-3-ene or but-2-ene DO show geometric isomerism
steps.narration: A double bond alone is not enough for geometric isomerism. Both carbons of the double bond must carry two different groups. Terminal alkenes ending in C H two have two identical hydrogens on one carbon, so only internal alkenes like hex-three-ene qualify.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Longest chain gives the root, functional group gives the suffix, lowest numbering places branches and multiple bonds, and same formula with different layout gives isomers.
working: Root (chain) + lowest locants + suffix (family)  |  Check formula first for isomers
steps.narration: Find the longest chain for the root, use the main functional group for the suffix, number for the lowest locants, and check both formula and connectivity to spot isomers.

options.why: Each carbon of the double bond in hex-3-ene carries a hydrogen and an ethyl group. Restricted rotation therefore allows distinct geometric isomers.
Hexane has no double bond to restrict rotation.
Prop-1-ene has two hydrogens on the terminal alkene carbon.
3-Methylbut-1-ene also has two hydrogens on its terminal alkene carbon.

steps.title: Diced yam and balanced crowds
steps.display:
Smaller pieces cook faster (reaction rate)
Equal people entering and leaving a hall (equilibrium)
steps.narration: Diced yam boils faster than a whole tuber because more surface meets hot water. Equilibrium is like a busy market where people enter and leave at equal speeds.

steps.title: Reaction rate and collision theory
steps.display:
Rate = \frac{Δ(concentration or volume)}{Δt}
Effective collision: E ≥ E_{a} AND proper orientation
working: Steepest upward slope on a volume–time curve = fastest rate
Horizontal flat part of the curve = reaction has stopped (rate = 0)
Activation energy (E_{a}) = minimum energy barrier for reaction
steps.narration: Reaction rate measures how fast reactant or product amount changes per unit time. By collision theory, particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy and with proper orientation.

steps.title: Factors affecting reaction rate
steps.display: Higher T, concentration, gas pressure, or surface area → faster rate
working: Concentration or gas pressure ↑ → more particles per volume → more collisions
Powder > chips > lump → larger solid surface area → shorter reaction time
Temperature ↑ → faster motion and more particles with E ≥ E_{a}
Nature of reactants: aqueous ionic reactions are faster than covalent ones; light aids photolysis
steps.narration: Increasing temperature, concentration, gas pressure, or solid surface area raises the frequency of effective collisions. Ionic reactions in solution are usually faster than covalent ones, and sunlight drives photochemical reactions.

steps.title: Catalysts and enzymes
steps.display: Catalyst lowers E_{a} via an alternative path (regenerated unchanged)
working: Lowers forward and reverse E_{a} equally → equilibrium reached faster
Does NOT change ΔH, total product yield, or equilibrium composition
Enzymes are biological catalysts (e.g. zymase; dehydrogenase in redox)
steps.narration: A positive catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated unchanged. It speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally without changing total yield or equilibrium position.

steps.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
steps.display: aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD  |  Rate_{forward} = Rate_{reverse} ≠ 0
working: Requires a closed system so gases or vapour cannot escape
Concentrations remain constant (not necessarily equal)
K_{c} = \frac{[C]^{c}[D]^{d}}{[A]^{a}[B]^{b}}  (exclude pure solids and liquids)
steps.narration: In a closed reversible reaction, dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates. Concentrations stay steady even though both reactions continue, and pure solids are omitted from K c.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle (concentration, pressure, temperature)
steps.display: Stress applied → equilibrium shifts to oppose the stress
working: Concentration: add reactant or remove product → shifts right; add common ion → shifts away
Pressure ↑ (gases): shifts toward FEWER gas moles (if equal gas moles, no shift)
Temperature ↑: favours endothermic direction (ΔH > 0); ONLY temperature changes K_{c}
Inert gas added at constant volume: no shift in equilibrium position
steps.narration: Le Chatelier's principle states that an equilibrium shifts to counteract any change in concentration, gas pressure, or temperature. Only temperature alters the equilibrium constant, while adding an inert gas at constant volume gives no shift.

steps.title: Write the equilibrium constant K_{c}
working: Given at equilibrium: [SO_{2}] = 0.2, [O_{2}] = 0.5, [SO_{3}] = 0.4 mol dm^{−3}
Put products on top and reactants below, each raised to its coefficient
steps.narration: Write the equilibrium constant K c for sulphur four oxide, sulfur dioxide, reacting with oxygen to form sulphur six oxide, sulfur trioxide. Place product concentrations over reactants, raised to their coefficients.

steps.title: Substitute equilibrium concentrations
steps.narration: Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the expression. Zero point four squared gives zero point one six on top, while zero point two squared times zero point five gives zero point zero two below.

steps.title: Compute K_{c} and check units
steps.narration: Divide zero point one six by zero point zero two to obtain eight. Because there are two concentration powers above and three below, the unit is per mole cubic decimetre.

steps.title: Predict pressure shift at constant T
steps.display:
Reactants: 2 + 1 = 3 mol gas  |  Product: 2 mol gas
Higher P → shifts right; K_{c} stays 8
working: Compression favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 < 3)
Constant temperature keeps K_{c} unchanged at 8 mol^{−1} dm^{3}
steps.narration: Count gas moles on both sides. Three moles of reactant gas form two moles of product gas, so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium right, while K c stays eight at constant temperature.

steps.title: Read the JAMB question
steps.display:
For the exothermic equilibrium P(g) + Q(g) ⇌ 3R(s) + S(g),
which change increases the yield of R?
working: States matter: P, Q, S are gases (g), while R is a solid (s)
Gas moles: 2 mol on left (P + Q) vs 1 mol on right (S only)
steps.narration: In this JAMB question, gases P and Q react exothermically to form solid R and gas S. Check vessel size, temperature, removing S, and a catalyst to see which increases R.

steps.title: Test using a larger closed vessel
steps.display: Larger vessel → lower pressure → favours more gas moles
working: Left has 2 mol gas; right has 1 mol gas (ignore solid R)
Equilibrium shifts left → yield of R decreases
steps.narration: Using a larger closed vessel lowers the pressure, which favours the side with more gas molecules. Ignoring solid R leaves two gas moles on the left against one on the right, shifting left.

steps.title: Test increasing the temperature
steps.display: Forward is exothermic (ΔH < 0) → reverse is endothermic
working: Heating favours the endothermic reverse direction
Equilibrium shifts left → yield of R decreases
steps.narration: Because the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction absorbs heat. Increasing the temperature therefore favours the endothermic reverse direction, shifting left and reducing the yield of R.

steps.title: Test catalyst and removing S
steps.display:
Positive catalyst: no change in equilibrium yield
Removing S(g): equilibrium shifts right → more R(s)
