working: A positive catalyst speeds forward and reverse rates equally
Removing gaseous S pulls equilibrium right to replace S, forming more R
steps.narration: Adding a positive catalyst speeds up both directions equally without changing the equilibrium yield. Removing gaseous S disturbs the balance and shifts equilibrium right to replace it, producing more solid R.

steps.title: Catalysts never increase total yield or shift equilibrium
steps.display:
Wrong: Catalyst makes more total product or shifts equilibrium right
Right: Catalyst only lowers E_{a}, reaching the same yield sooner
working: Equal H_{2}O_{2} samples give equal total O_{2} with or without MnO_{2}
Forward and reverse activation energies drop equally, so K_{c} is unchanged
steps.narration: Do not assume a catalyst creates extra product or favours the forward side. A catalyst lowers activation energy equally in both directions, so equilibrium arrives sooner with the exact same yield.

steps.title: Count only gases for pressure, and watch equal gas moles
steps.display:
Wrong: Pressure always shifts equilibrium, or solids count as gas volume
Right: Count only (g) moles; equal gas moles (Δn = 0) → no shift
working: A(g) ⇌ B(g) or H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): equal gas moles → no shift
2CO(g) + O_{2}(g) ⇌ 2CO_{2}(g): 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas → compression shifts right
steps.narration: Never assume compression always favours products or counts solids. Count only gaseous coefficients on each side, and remember that equal gas moles on both sides give no shift under pressure.

steps.title: Equilibrium is dynamic, and temperature changes K_{c}
steps.display:
Wrong: Reactions stop at equilibrium, or K_{c} never changes
Right: Forward and reverse rates stay equal; heating changes K_{c}
working: Exothermic forward (ΔH < 0): heating shifts left → K_{c} decreases
Endothermic forward (ΔH > 0): heating shifts right → K_{c} increases
steps.narration: At equilibrium, opposing reactions have not stopped and concentrations need not be equal; only their rates match. Also remember that changing temperature alters the equilibrium constant, decreasing it for exothermic reactions.

steps.title: Collisions set speed; opposition sets shift
steps.display:
Rate ↑ with effective collisions per second
Equilibrium opposes stress; only temperature alters K_{c}
steps.narration: Reaction rate grows when more collisions clear the activation energy with proper orientation, while a closed equilibrium always shifts to oppose stress without a catalyst changing the final yield.

quickCheck.stem: Which combination gives the highest rate of carbon dioxide production?

options.text: 0.05 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses powder but a weaker acid concentration.

options.text: 0.05 mol dm^{−3} HCl and a 5 g lump of CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses both a lower concentration and a lump with less exposed surface.

options.text: 0.10 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: Powder exposes more calcium carbonate surface, and the 0.10 mol dm^{−3} acid has the highest concentration. Together these give the highest collision rate and fastest carbon dioxide production.

options.text: 0.025 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses powder with the lowest acid concentration listed.

steps.title: Cooking firewood and instant cold packs
steps.display:
Burning firewood → heat flows out (warms the pot)
Cold pack salt dissolving → heat flows in (chills your hand)
steps.narration: Burning firewood pushes heat out into your cooking pot and kitchen air. Dissolving an instant cold pack pulls heat from your hand, making the pack feel chilly.

steps.title: Exothermic, endothermic and sign of ΔH
steps.display:
ΔH = ΣH_{products} − ΣH_{reactants}
Exothermic: ΔH < 0  |  Endothermic: ΔH > 0
working: Exothermic: heat released to surroundings → temperature rises (ΔH is −)
Endothermic: heat absorbed from surroundings → temperature falls (ΔH is +)
Carbon(IV) oxide (carbon dioxide): C(s) + O_{2}(g) → CO_{2}(g), ΔH° = −393 kJ mol^{−1}
steps.narration: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings, so products hold less enthalpy and delta H is negative. Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings, so delta H is positive.

steps.title: Energy profile diagrams
steps.display:
Exothermic: E_{products} < E_{reactants} (step down)
Endothermic: E_{products} > E_{reactants} (step up)
working: Top of the curve = transition state (activated complex)
Activation energy: E_{a} = E_{peak} − E_{reactants} (always positive)
Enthalpy arrow: from reactant level to product level (ΔH = E_{products} − E_{reactants})
steps.narration: On an energy profile diagram, reactants climb over an activation energy barrier to reach products. Exothermic products end lower than reactants, whereas endothermic products end higher than reactants.

steps.title: Heats of reaction, combustion and neutralisation
steps.display: q = m c ΔT  |  ΔH = ± \frac{q}{n}
working: Combustion (ΔH_{c}°): 1 mol burns completely in excess O_{2} (always −)
Neutralisation (ΔH_{n}°): 1 mol H_{2}O formed; strong acid + strong base = −57.3 kJ mol^{−1}
Weak acid or base gives |ΔH_{n}°| < 57.3 kJ mol^{−1} (ionisation absorbs heat)
Water c = 4.2 or 4.18 J g^{−1} K^{−1} (use the value given in the question)
steps.narration: Standard heat of combustion burns one mole completely in excess oxygen and is always exothermic. Standard neutralisation forms one mole of water, releasing fifty-seven point three kilojoules per mole for strong acids and strong bases.

steps.title: Heat of solution and Hess's law
steps.display: ΔH_{soln} = ΔH_{lattice dissociation} + ΔH_{hyd}
working: Breaking the crystal lattice absorbs energy (+); hydrating ions releases energy (−)
Hydration energy > lattice separation energy → exothermic (ΔH_{soln} < 0)
Hess's law: total ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the route
steps.narration: Dissolving an ionic salt absorbs energy to separate the lattice and releases hydration energy when water surrounds the ions. By Hess's law, overall enthalpy change depends only on initial and final states.

steps.title: Bond energies and spontaneity
steps.display: ΔH = ΣE(bonds broken) − ΣE(bonds formed)
working: Breaking reactant bonds absorbs energy (endothermic, +)
Forming product bonds releases energy (exothermic, −)
Spontaneity check: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (ΔG < 0 spontaneous; T in K = °C + 273)
steps.narration: Breaking chemical bonds always absorbs energy, while forming new bonds always releases energy. Subtract the energy released forming product bonds from the energy absorbed breaking reactant bonds to estimate delta H.

steps.title: Count bonds broken and formed
working: Bonds broken in reactants: 1 H−H bond and 1 Cl−Cl bond
Bonds formed in products: 2 H−Cl bonds
steps.narration: Estimate delta H when hydrogen gas and chlorine gas form hydrogen chloride. Count one hydrogen-hydrogen bond and one chlorine-chlorine bond broken in the reactants, and two hydrogen-chlorine bonds formed in the products.

steps.title: Sum energy absorbed breaking bonds
steps.display: ΣE(bonds broken) = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
working: Bond breaking is endothermic (+)
steps.narration: Add the bond energies of the reactants to find the energy absorbed. Four hundred and thirty-six plus two hundred and forty-two gives six hundred and seventy-eight kilojoules.

steps.title: Sum energy released forming bonds
steps.display: ΣE(bonds formed) = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ
working: Two moles of H−Cl form, so multiply 431 by 2
steps.narration: Multiply the hydrogen-chlorine bond energy by two because two moles of hydrogen chloride form. Two times four hundred and thirty-one equals eight hundred and sixty-two kilojoules released.

steps.title: Subtract formed from broken
working: 862 kJ released > 678 kJ absorbed → net exothermic
steps.narration: Subtract energy released from energy absorbed. Six hundred and seventy-eight minus eight hundred and sixty-two gives minus one hundred and eighty-four kilojoules, showing an exothermic reaction.

steps.title: Read the JAMB question
steps.display:
At 25°C, a system has a free energy change of −899 J mol^{−1} and an entropy change of 10 J mol^{−1} K^{−1}.
Calculate the enthalpy change.
working: Given: t = 25 °C, ΔG = −899 J mol^{−1}, ΔS = 10 J mol^{−1} K^{−1}
Required: ΔH in J mol^{−1}
steps.narration: This JAMB question gives free energy change as minus eight hundred and ninety-nine joules per mole and entropy change as ten joules per mole per kelvin at twenty-five degrees Celsius.

steps.title: Convert Celsius to Kelvin
working: JAMB convention uses T(K) = t(°C) + 273
Both ΔG and ΔS are already in joules, so no kJ conversion is needed
steps.narration: Convert temperature to kelvin first by adding two hundred and seventy-three. Twenty-five plus two hundred and seventy-three equals two hundred and ninety-eight kelvin, and the joule units already match.

steps.title: Rearrange the free energy equation
steps.display: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS  ⇒  ΔH = ΔG + TΔS
steps.narration: Rearrange the Gibbs free energy formula so delta H equals delta G plus T delta S. Multiply two hundred and ninety-eight by ten to get two thousand nine hundred and eighty joules per mole.

steps.title: Substitute and find ΔH
working: +2980 exceeds −899, giving a positive (endothermic) ΔH
steps.narration: Add minus eight hundred and ninety-nine and two thousand nine hundred and eighty. That gives plus two thousand and eighty-one joules per mole, matching the positive value.

steps.title: Never reverse bond-energy or profile signs
steps.display:
Wrong: ΔH = ΣE(formed) − ΣE(broken), or exothermic products higher
Right: ΔH = ΣE(broken) − ΣE(formed); exothermic products sit lower
working: Breaking a bond always absorbs energy (+)
Forming a bond always releases energy (−)
steps.narration: Do not flip the bond energy formula or profile heights. Breaking bonds always takes in energy and forming bonds always releases it, while exothermic products always sit below reactants.

steps.title: Convert °C to Kelvin and match energy units
steps.display:
Wrong: T = 25 in TΔS, or mixing kJ with J
Right: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K; keep ΔH and TΔS in matching units
working: Using 25 instead of 298 K gives −649 J mol^{−1} (a classic trap)
If ΔH is in kJ and ΔS is in J K^{−1}, divide ΔS by 1000
steps.narration: Always convert degrees Celsius to kelvin before multiplying by delta S, because using twenty-five instead of two hundred and ninety-eight leads straight to a trap value. Also match joules with joules.

steps.title: Cold surroundings mean endothermic, not exothermic
steps.display:
Wrong: Solution turns cold → heat left system (ΔH < 0)
Right: Solution turns cold → system absorbed heat (ΔH > 0); check ΔG for spontaneity
working: Cold pack cools water and hand because dissolving absorbs heat (ΔH > 0)
Exothermic ΔH < 0 alone does not guarantee spontaneity; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides
steps.narration: When a beaker feels cold, the reacting particles pulled heat from the water and surroundings, so delta H is positive. Also remember exothermic enthalpy alone never decides spontaneity without checking delta G.

steps.title: Follow the heat flow
steps.narration: Always track whether heat enters or leaves the reacting system. Heat leaving gives negative delta H and lower product energy, while heat absorbed gives positive delta H and higher product energy.

quickCheck.stem: What describes dissolution of an ionic solid when the energy released by hydration exceeds the energy required to separate the lattice?

options.why: Spontaneity also depends on the entropy change.
An endothermic process has a positive enthalpy change.
The solution enthalpy is the positive lattice separation energy plus the negative hydration enthalpy. The net enthalpy change is negative.
Reversibility cannot be determined from the two energy magnitudes alone.
